explanations.answer: To save him by His name
explanations.explanation: That's the very first thing out of his mouth, friend: "Save me, O God, by Your name, and vindicate me by Your might!" He doesn't open with a plan or a complaint. He goes straight to God and asks for rescue. I think that tells you where he knew help would come from.

explanations.answer: To hide him from Saul's army
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd pick it, since David is in hiding and the Ziphites just gave him away. But the text never mentions an army, and he never asks God to hide him. He says, "Save me, O God, by Your name, and vindicate me by Your might!" The song opens with a cry for rescue, not a hiding spot.

Nice thought, baker, but David never asks for that here. He prays, "Save me, O God, by Your name, and vindicate me by Your might!" He wants to be saved and vindicated, and Saul's forgiveness never comes up in this song. Sometimes I add extra chips to a recipe that never asked for them, so I get the urge.

explanations.answer: Ruthless men are out to take his life
explanations.explanation: There it is. David says, "For strangers rise up against me, and ruthless men seek my life—men with no regard for God." Those words are why he's begging God to hear him. When somebody is after your life, you don't pray a casual little prayer, friend.

explanations.answer: His own family has turned against him
explanations.explanation: This song never says that. David says "…strangers rise up against me, and ruthless men seek my life…" Strangers, baker, not family. So the pleading comes from men who want his life, not from any family trouble.

explanations.answer: He has fallen sick and can't get up
explanations.explanation: David doesn't mention being sick anywhere in this song. He says, "For strangers rise up against me, and ruthless men seek my life…" His trouble is men who seek his life, not an illness.

Careful, friend, this one is the opposite of what David says. Right after the Selah he says, "Surely God is my helper; the Lord is the sustainer of my soul." He doesn't say God left him alone. He says God is his helper. The song turns right there.

Right, it's false. After the Selah, David says, "Surely God is my helper; the Lord is the sustainer of my soul." No abandonment anywhere, just a man declaring that God helps him and sustains him. That's a big shift in the middle of a scary song.

Not quite, baker. David hands the matter to God, saying, "He will reward my enemies with evil." The "He" there is God, not David. So David isn't grabbing the payback himself, he's leaving it with God.
Yes, it's false. David says of God, "He will reward my enemies with evil." He doesn't say "I will." He puts it in God's hands, which, honestly, is a better spot for it than mine.
That's the promise. David says, "Freely I will sacrifice to You…" That word freely stands out to me. I think he means it as a gift he's glad to give, not something he's dragged into.

explanations.answer: Build Him a house of cedar
explanations.explanation: That's a good-sounding answer, but it's not in this song. David's promise here is, "Freely I will sacrifice to You…" He never mentions building a house of cedar in this psalm. Here it's just a free sacrifice.
Forty days without eating? I'd be fainting by day two, friend, and cookies would be calling my name. But David never promises that here. He says, "Freely I will sacrifice to You…"
Yes, he does. David says, "I will praise Your name, O LORD, for it is good." He gives the reason right in the promise: the name is good. So he's got a sacrifice and some praise lined up.
Look again, baker, because it's right there in verse 6. David says, "I will praise Your name, O LORD, for it is good." He promises praise and gives the reason too. So this one is true.
That's the closing reason. David says, "For He has delivered me from every trouble…" Every trouble, friend, not just the easy ones. That's a lot of praise material.

explanations.answer: Made him king over all Israel
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since David did become king of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3). But that's not what he sings about here. He closes with, "For He has delivered me from every trouble…" The reason for his praise is deliverance.

explanations.answer: Given him a city of his own
explanations.explanation: A city of his own would be nice, but this song doesn't say it. David says, "For He has delivered me from every trouble…" That's the reason he gives for his praise. No real estate in this one, baker.
Not what the song says, friend. David says, "…my eyes have looked in triumph on my foes." That's triumph, not fear. He's looking at them with his head up.
Right, it's false. David says, "…my eyes have looked in triumph on my foes." The man who started the song begging for rescue ends it looking in triumph. Quite the change, baker.
